Endangered Species BY JOE FORDHAM A t the conclusion of 20th Century Fox's 2014 Dawn of the Planet of the Apes, the fate of Caesar (Andy Serkis), leader of the genetically-enhanced apes, was uncertain. "I knew that we were ending on the precipice of war," remarked the film's director, Matt Reeves. ¿And I knew that I wanted the next film to be about Caesar becoming the seminal figure in ape history, taking him to a place where he would become virtually an ape Moses. But exactly what that story was, I didn't know. On Dawn, Reeves had hit the ground running, inheriting the project from Rupert Wyatt, director of the previous Rise of the Planet of the Apes. As a lifelong fan of the Apes films, Reeves connected with the material and its mythological themes. Teamed with Weta Digital senior visual effects supervisor Joe Letteri, visual effects supervisor Dan Lemmon, production designer James Chinlund, and cinematographer Michael Seresin, Reeves told the story of Caesar's struggle leading an ape colony out of a peaceful existence in the rainforests of Muir Woods to assert its dominance over the human survivors of a 'simian virus' pandemic. 1 / 30 Critics and fans embraced the film as an intelligent and deeply-felt addition to the
War for the Planet of the Apes

saga. The film received an Oscar nomination for its visual effects, and earned Reeves APES 3 and his screenwriter Mark Bomback time to devise Caesar's next chapter. We started watching movies and discussed how to tell a story that felt like a Biblical epic for an ape," said Reeves. ¿We watched Ben-Hur and The Ten Commandments, and all of the old Apes films. On Dawn, we didn't have time to watch all of the films - and I have to confess, although I'm a huge Planet of the Apes fan, I don't know that I'd ever seen Battle for the Planet of the Apes, which many fans thought we'd be doing next. When Mark and I watched that, we were shocked by how many story elements were reflected in that film." Cinematic touchstones included The Bridge on the River Kwai, Paths of Glory, Apalypse Now and The Outlaw Josey Wales - war films with a focus on character. The secret of Rise was that it had been Caesar's movie, even more than Dawn, Reeves noted. I wanted to take that further and make an ape point-of-view movie, where the audience experienced the story through Caesar. I didn't want to cut away to human stories that weren't experienced through the apes. Caesar is on a quest, like the characters in Apocalypse Now, and we used the backdrop of a war epic to tell an intimate character storyi War for the Planet of the Apes begins two years after Dawn, as a renegade platoon of human soldiers and indentured ape trackers bearing an Alpha-Omega brand assault a heavily-fortified forest refuge where apes have retrenched. The surprise attack results in a crippling blow to Caesar (Serkis) when the troopers' ape-hating Colonel McCullough (Woody Harrelson) callously murders Caesar's wife and son. Knowing that the colony's safety has been compromised, Caesar orders his followers to head for a rumored far-off 2 / 30 Promised Land while he embarks on a revenge mission, seeking the Colonel, assisted

by his orangutan advisor Maurice (harin honoval), the gorilla Luca (Michael Adamthwaite), chimpanzee Rocket (Terry Notary) and a pair of unlikely companions that join a quest to liberate an ape prison labor camp. series, iwe have grand ambitions for what we want to accomplish. Half of that involves learning details that we didn't even know we needed to improve. Each film required different focuses, new characters and themes, and different tones. Dawn had a Shakespearean sprawl of characters, with themes of betrayal and leadership, and Caesar fighting for the survival of his family and his tribe. In War, the stakes were even higher. Caesar is fighting for his very soul, and Andy Serkis went beyond the ground he trod before. That required us to get back under the hood and rebuild significant sections of our facial puppet to hit the detail and subtlety of his performance." While the filmmakers returned to techniques established on Rise and Dawn - with performers authoring ape action largely on location using motion capture suits, witness cameras, clean plates, and motion capture pickups - the increased focus on apes required advanced logistics. "One of the most distinct differences between Dawn and War was the degree to which the production involved visual effects," noted visual effects producer Ryan Stafford, on his seventh year with the franchise. "On Dawn, we had apes in 70 percent of our shots. On War, 95 percent of our shots involved apes or visual effects. APES 3 he script took Weta Digital's performance capture technology into harsh new realms of combat, and dove deeper into Caesar's psyche. "Every time we go into one of these projects, remarked Dan Lemmon, three-time veteran of the 3 / 30

APES 3 I made recommendations on camera equipment, shooting platforms, how set components functioned with interactive elements that might impede our ability to add apes. Dan Lemmon and I worked very closely on scheduling. It was a huge collaboration because all of the production decisions impacted us greatly. The reliance on location photography inspired the filmmakers to pursue even more realism. "My theory was that if we shot in natural light it would only make the apes look more realistic," recalled Matt Reeves. "Weta completely agreed with that and, in every possible instance, I urged James Chinlund to build practical sets that we could put apes into. I wanted to push out of Muir Woods across the landscape of California, crossing the Sierras and into the snow to create an almost mythic setting. I felt we should adopt a grand and epic David Lean mode of filmmaking, where characters were dwarfed by the landscape, and so we shot almost entirely on location." The filmmakers also built partial soundstage elements at Mammoth Studios in Vancouver. "While Mark Bomback and I were writing," said Reeves, "we watched Kurosawa's The Hidden Fortress and we decided the apes could adapt their new refuge in Muir Woods inside catacombs behind a waterfall. James Chinlund designed an enormous set just outside of the realm of possibility for our budget. Dan Lemmon suggested building smaller parts for real and that gave Weta enough texture to flesh out scenes for the other parts of the catacombs. That was one of our only scenes shot on a virtual set, but the parts we built gave us textures so we would match to something real, shot in natural lighti Naturalistic lighting played into the strengths of Weta's raytracer, Manuka. Manuka 4 / 30 has made a huge difference to the way shots look," commented Joe Letteri. "When we
War for the Planet of the Apes

introduced Manuka on Dawn, we only used it for background characters; one of its strengths was being able to handle large scenes, and we used it to churn through backgrounds. This time, we handled everything through Manuka, and it really shone in closeups, bringing out the lighting. In larger synthetic environments, it allowed us to integrate renders where it felt like everything belonged to the same world. Manuka helped us fully understand the physics of lighting captured on set, which allowed for a nice integration between live-action and rendered elements." looked much more realistic in performance passes," said Matt Reeves. "I asked Ryan and Weta to bring that into our visual effects budget, and we approached ape interactions intentionally using performance passes. We always shot a clean pass - and the artists at Weta did amazing work with some very labor intensive paint-outs - but using the performance pass was much better for the actors on both sides of the CG divide." Weta Digital updated performance capture tools, which motion capture supervisor Dejan Momcilovic employed using LED active markers on ape performer suits, with Standard Deviation motion sensor cameras, a combination of Giant software, custom facial recording tools and Autodesk MotionBuilder on-set visualization. ¿Probably the most complicated part of the process this time was that our access on set was impaired by the snow," said Dan Lemmon. "The LED markers could shine through falling snow and, APES 3 he emphasis on in-camera realism informed shooting methodology, which relied on motion capture passes with ape actors as production plates, often requiring challenging digital paint-outs to add animated apes. APES 3 in some cases, they blasted right through clothing. But it was a challenge shooting in the forests of British Columbia where we were sometimes up to our waists in snow drifts. Facial camera rigs were half the size of the helmet-mounted cameras used on Dawn. "The cameras sat on a boom on the front of the helmets and pointed back up into the actor's faces. We switched to infrared LEDS, rather than white light LEDS, so it was not distracting for the actor. And when we were shooting darker setups, the light didn't contaminate the set.i To assist his interpretation of Caesar, Andy Serkis added weights to his motion capture wardrobe. "Andy wore sandbag cuffs around his ankles," noted animation supervisor Dan Barrett. ¿That weighed his feet down to make him appear more wearied. Caesar was still very vital, but he was showing his age a little. We used essentially the same face puppet, but we made him a little grayer, with more wrinkling. Andy's performance was so strong and nuanced, Matt allowed the camera to linger on Caesar, which really brought out the characteri Refinements to animation tools allowed more nuances in facial animation.iWe had mastered the main difficulties of translating from performers to apesi said facial modeling supervisor Alessandro Bonora, so we had more time to focus on subtleties. Using Manuka, and new versions of our Gazebo plugin, helped animators play with the puppets twice as fast. All those evolutions of tools, plus our experience of the last two films, made the experience more streamlined and allowed us to concentrate on refining the work. Weta Digital creature teams built new apes using a flexible approach to modeling 6 / 30 and underlying tissue technology. "We now have better skin sliding and simulations and
War for the Planet of the Apes

a better facial solver," said muscle and skin supervisor Tim Forbes. "That gave us a good foundation upon which to create all the characters. We applied developments to different ape anatomies. And because we were using the models across different archetypes, it was a very efficient way to build numerous shapes and sizes of characters, whether they were chimps, orangutan, gorilla, or even humans. We could migrate data to build a diverse array of characters, which was very useful for battles and crowd scenesi fur supervisor Andrea Merlo. i"We've added a new dynamic engine that allowed us to do better collisions and interactions with wind, water and debris, and we simulated more hairs to create more precise simulations." Cold climates added to the complexity of fur behavior. On Dawn we simulated rain droplets on individual fur strands, which was pretty complex. Snow has another characteristic where particles bridge the gaps between clumps of fur and accumulate into larger clumps. We had to figure out what the snow was doing to each hair, and how to make hairs react in groups. We had simulations for snow accumulating on the characters as they were fighting and rolling around in the snowi New 'donkey' apes in servitude to Alpha-Omega included the russet-pelted gorilla, Red (Ty Olsson), and an albino gorilla named Winter (Aleks Paunovic). Weta Digital created character models based on reference of Winston, a silverback in San Diego Zoo Safari Park, for Red; and Snowflake, a white-pelted ape who had been a key character APES 3 ur grooms made use of Wig, an evolution of Weta Digital's Barbershop technology used on Dawn, incorporating more dynamic controls.It's a little bit faster and allowed us to interface with our new dynamic engine a little bit betteri said 7 / 30

APES 3 reference for Peter Jackson's King Kong, for Winter.Our two new hero gorillas gave us the chance to rework our gorilla setup,i noted modeling supervisor Florian Fernandez. "We created a realistic bone structure that we fitted to each gorilla and on top of that we built a full muscle system. We then refitted the skeleton into a different framework for each character, adjusted bones and muscle volumes, and did fine adjustments for skin thickness and simulations." The modeling paradigm allowed changes mid-stream. "Red changed a few times in script. He used to be a chimp. He became a gorilla, initially, because the motion capture performer was quite a bulky guy and as a chimp we weren't able to cover up the screen space Ty occupied. When we made him a larger character, it was not such a heavy paint-out to cover the performer in the plate, and his gorilla stature worked much better for Red's intimidating character. Caesar's quest introduced a key character in Bad Ape (Steve Zahn), a wizened chimpanzee refugee from a zoo. "We wanted to introduce an ape who hadn't been raised as part of Caesar's community," said Matt Reeves, "the implication being that there are many more apes out there. Mark Bomback and I found a picture of a chimp that we used to pitch our story to the studio. Bad Ape is a heartbreaking hermit who lives in an old ski lodge, which looks like the ice chalet from Dr. Zhivago, where he has retreated after the viral apocalypse when he witnessed humans killing apes. He's been hiding there so long, all he really wants is to have a friend. The character inspired an empathic performance. "Steve Zahn connected to the character in a very emotional way. He first read some scenes for me over Skype and I was very moved. I knew he'd be funny, but he was 8 / 30 so touching. The animators drew out his performance from the character that Steve cre-
War for the Planet of the Apes

ated on set.i A plate, and we made sure that all of Bad Ape's character traits in that picture played into our puppet. Interestingly, when we looked at the other views of the same ape, we found that some aspects of the real ape's face fought the character that Matt was going for, so we ended up returning to that single front-on view. We thinned down his jaw quite a bit to give him a slightly narrower neck. And his body was unlike a typical old chimpanzee. His anatomy was closer to an eight- or nine-year-old, skinnier and scrawnier, but we played him as much older, with a frail innocence. Bad Ape's physiognomy posed artistic challenges in adapting Zahn's performance. There are times when we try to work the likeness of a performer into a digital character. Signature wrinkles and telltale changes in an actor's face can help connect a digital character emotionally to an actor. A lot of times it's more about the change than it is the rest-pose; if you can get the changes to read, the character's performance tends to feel like the actor. That was key for Bad Ape. We focused on the changes in Steve Zahn's face, and we made sure those mapped across to Bad Ape, even though the ape didn't resemble Steve physically." Florian Fernandez's team modeled Bad Ape using combinations of Autodesk Mudbox, Maya and Pixologic ZBrush. Andrea Merlo's team developed a system that coupled a sparse hair groom with cloth simulations of Bad Ape's woolen hat and human winter APES 3I aron Sims Creative developed Bad Ape's design, emphasizing the character's fragility.iThere was a particular image of Bad Ape making a facial expression that Matt fell in love with," recalled Dan Lemmon. "We used that as our tem9 / 30

APES 3 clothing, and with nature reference of skin textures. "Patchy skin is quite typical for a chimp," noted Tim Forbes. "That gave us some nice effects of how his skin slid over the underlying anatomy. He was such a featured character, we put a lot of work into highresolution skin-slide, muscle flexing, and especially his facial rig. To develop facial articulation, Steve Zahn performed a range of contortions, which Weta adapted to Bad Ape's facial rig. "Steve shared some similarities with Andy Serkis," noted Alessandro Bonora.iIn his levator labii - which are muscles that curl the upper lip - when Steve cranked up to full sneer, he barely showed any upper teeth. That was tricky to apply to Bad Ape because, when chimps sneer, they tend to show upper teeth and gums to the junction between the gum and upper lip. That's where the translation game began, and we applied appropriate ranges in our puppet to help the animators match Bad Ape's face to Steve's, judging how to give the character weight and life. The puppet featured a detailed eye model. "All our characters got new eyeballs. On top of that, we developed new deformers that helped keep eyelids tight to the eyeball, with a new model for the meniscus water layer covering the eyeball. Facial animation lead Jack Tema then weighed Bad Ape's intelligence and simian traits. "Steve did a fantastic 'chimpy' performance," observed Dan Barrett. "It was a lovely, comic turn, but bittersweet. It said a lot about the character that he happily used the name 'Bad Ape' although his abusive handlers had given him that name. But he retained a positive outlook, and that was an absolute delight to convey from Steve Zahn's performance. We hadn't seen a character like him before in the Apes universe. He was 10 / 30 physically small, but a brave little character who finds his inner hero. That was one of
War for the Planet of the Apes

the biggest things we took from Steve's performance - the way he took in the world and the way he expressed his fears and occasional nervousness. It's all there in his big beautiful eyes." F plained Dan Lemmon. The location had sheer rock cliffs, tunnels and a raging river going by. We added a waterfall, and behind the waterfall we staged the ape fortress interior, most of which we created as a digital environment, apart from portions - including Caesar's dwelling near the top of the waterfall - that James Chinlund designed and built as sets." To plan the sequence, Halon Entertainment incorporated production plans and animated assets into a new previsualization pipeline.iThis was our first time using the Unreal game engine for previs," noted Halon previs supervisor A.J. Briones. "It allowed us to drive more characters, create better lighting, and give our previs a more realistic look. We made use of Weta's lidar data, as well as the production designer's Maya and Rhino modeling files as a starting point when creating our previs environments. Unreal gave us a lot more tools to create great looking previs. We also adapted the motion capture data of our animation pipeline to work with Weta's timecode-based motion capture data, which proved extremely valuable, especially in postvis." The attack begins as Alpha-Omega troopers open fire with rocket propelled grenades, APES 3 or the opening attack on the Hidden Fortress, the production shot scenes in a • disused quarry near Othello, in Coquihalla Canyon Provincial Park, British Columbia. "The Hidden Fortress is an ape village hidden behind a waterfall," ex11 / 30

APES 3 and apes respond with gunfire, arrows and homemade bombs. Stunt coordinator John Stoneham initiated ape and soldier interactions on set, while the special effects team staged pyrotechnic effects.
